ja: だいさんじゅうよんかい

p.src: After Lady Jia, Lady Wang, and the others had left, Xiren came over, sat beside Baoyu, and asked him through her tears, “How did it ever come to such a beating?” Baoyu sighed. “It was only over those old matters. What is the use of asking about them? Only my lower half hurts terribly. Take a look and see whether anything there has been badly injured.” At this, Xiren gently slipped in her hand and eased down his undergarment. Whenever Baoyu moved even slightly, he clenched his teeth and cried, “Ai-yo!” Xiren hurriedly stopped, and it took three or four attempts before she finally got the garment off. When Xiren examined him, she saw that the upper parts of his thighs were black and blue, with swollen, rigid welts fully four fingers wide. Gritting her teeth, Xiren exclaimed, “Merciful heavens! How could anyone strike so viciously? If only you had listened to one word of mine, things would never have come to this. Fortunately, no bones or sinews were damaged. But what would we do if the beating had left you crippled?” As she spoke, they heard the maids announce, “Miss Bao is here.” Hearing this and knowing there was no time to put his undergarment back on, Xiren took a lined gauze quilt and covered Baoyu with it. Baochai entered with a medicinal pill resting in her palm and said to Xiren, “This evening, grind this medicine in wine and apply it to him. It will disperse the heat and poison of the congealed blood, and then he should soon recover.” With that, she handed it to Xiren and asked, “Are you feeling any better now?” Baoyu thanked her and replied, “I am better.” He also invited her to sit down. Seeing him open his eyes and speak, unlike before, Baochai felt considerably relieved. She nodded and sighed. “If only you had listened to someone sooner, it would never have come to this. It is not only Grandmother and Mother who are distressed; even we feel pain when we see you like this.” She had barely said this before she hurriedly checked herself. Regretting that she had spoken too impulsively, she involuntarily blushed and lowered her head. Baoyu found her words so tender, intimate, and full of meaning. Then he saw her stop short, her face flushed and her head bowed as she kept toying with her sash. Her shy and delicate embarrassment was beyond description. His heart filled with delight, and he cast his pain far beyond the highest clouds, thinking, “I have suffered only a few blows, yet each of them reveals such pity and sorrow for me. Their feelings are delightful to savor and behold, and make them both lovable and worthy of reverence. If some sudden calamity were to befall me and I died a violent death, who knows how deeply they would grieve! Since they feel this way, even if I were to die at once, having won such devotion from them, I would have nothing to regret though all the endeavors of my life came to nothing. If my spirit did not rejoice contentedly in the dark world beyond, I should indeed be called a muddle-headed ghost.” While he was thinking this, he heard Baochai ask Xiren, “How did tempers suddenly flare when everything was well, and why did the beating begin?”

p.src: Xiren then repeated what Beiming had told her. Baoyu had known nothing of what Jia Huan had said and learned of it only when Xiren revealed it. When she also implicated Xue Pan, Baoyu feared Baochai might take offense and hurriedly stopped Xiren. “Cousin Xue has never been like that. You must not make wild guesses.” Hearing this, Baochai understood that he feared she would take it to heart and was using these words to silence Xiren. She thought privately, “Beaten into this state, he can scarcely attend to his own pain, yet he remains so considerate and fears offending others. It seems he does take some care over us. Since you are so thoughtful, why not devote that care to serious matters outside? Then your father would be pleased, and you would not suffer such punishment. You may have stopped Xiren because you feared I would be offended, but surely I know my own brother’s usual nature—willful, self-indulgent, and utterly heedless of consequences. He once turned the whole household upside down over Qin Zhong; naturally, he must be even more outrageous now than he was then.” Having thought this, she smiled and said, “There is no need for you to blame this person or that. In my view, the root of it is that Brother Bao usually behaves improperly and chooses to associate with those people, which made his father angry. Even if my brother spoke carelessly and happened to mention Brother Bao, he did not mean to incite anyone. For one thing, what he said was true; for another, he has never concerned himself with such niceties as avoiding suspicion. Miss Xiren, from childhood you have known only someone as thoughtful as Brother Bao. You have never met a man like my brother, who fears neither heaven nor earth and blurts out whatever is on his mind.” After mentioning Xue Pan and seeing Baoyu interrupt her, Xiren had already realized that she had spoken rashly. Afraid that Baochai might feel slighted, she was left still more ashamed and speechless by Baochai’s response. Hearing Baochai speak in this way—half with open propriety and half to dispel his suspicions—Baoyu felt more delighted than ever. Just as he was about to speak, Baochai rose and said, “I shall come to see you again tomorrow. Rest and recover properly. I have given the medicine I brought to Xiren. Once it is applied this evening, you are sure to improve.” With that, she walked out through the door. Xiren hurried after her and escorted her beyond the courtyard. “You have been very kind to trouble yourself, miss. When Second Master Bao has recovered, he will come and thank you in person.” Baochai looked back with a smile. “There is nothing to thank me for. Just persuade him to rest quietly and not indulge in wild imaginings; that will be enough. There is no need to alarm Grandmother, Mother, and everyone else. If word should drift into his father’s ears, nothing may happen at the moment, but when a similar occasion arises in the future, he will inevitably suffer for it.” As she spoke, she went on her way.

p.src: Xiren returned to the room, feeling deeply grateful to Baochai. When she entered and saw Baoyu lying silent and pensive, neither quite asleep nor awake, she withdrew again and went to wash and comb her hair. Baoyu lay silently on the bed, but the pain in his buttocks felt as if needles were piercing and knives gouging him, while the flesh burned as though scorched by fire. Whenever he shifted even slightly, he could not keep from crying, “Ai-yo!” By then evening was drawing near. Xiren had gone, but two or three maids were still in attendance. Since he had no need to call for anything, Baoyu said, “Go and wash and comb your hair for now. Come back when I call you.” They all obeyed and withdrew.

p.src: Baoyu lay there in a dazed stupor. He saw Jiang Yuhan enter and tell him how the Prince of Zhongshun's household had tried to seize him; then Jinchuan came in weeping and spoke of how she had thrown herself into the well because of him. Half dreaming and half awake, Baoyu paid no heed to any of it. Suddenly he felt someone pushing him, and through his haze he heard a person sobbing sorrowfully. Baoyu started awake from his dream and opened his eyes. It was none other than Lin Daiyu. Still fearing that he was dreaming, Baoyu hurriedly raised himself and peered closely at her face. Her eyes were swollen like two peaches and her whole face glistened with tears. If this was not Daiyu, who else could it be? Baoyu tried to look at her again, but the pain in the lower half of his body was unbearable. Unable to support himself, he cried, “Ow!” and fell back down. With a sigh he said, “What have you come running here for? Though the sun has gone down, the heat still lingers in the ground. Going back and forth like this, you may suffer heatstroke again—what would we do then? Although I was beaten, it does not hurt at all. I only put on this appearance to deceive them, so that word will spread outside and reach Father's ears. It is all an act, really. You mustn't take it seriously.” At that moment Daiyu was not wailing aloud, but her silent weeping, with her breath choking and her throat constricted, was all the more agonizing. After hearing Baoyu's words, she had ten thousand things in her heart to say, yet she could not utter a single one. Only after a long while did she manage to say between sobs, “From now on, please change your ways—all of them!” At this, Baoyu gave a long sigh and said, “Don't worry. You mustn't say such things. Even if I were to die for those people, I would do so willingly!” Before he had finished speaking, someone outside the courtyard announced, “Second Mistress is here.” Daiyu knew at once that Xifeng had come. She hurriedly rose and said, “I'll leave by the back courtyard and come again later.” Baoyu caught hold of her and said, “How strange! Why should you suddenly be afraid of her?” Daiyu stamped her foot in vexation and whispered, “Just look at my eyes! She would only make jokes about them to amuse herself.” Hearing this, Baoyu hastily released her. In a few quick steps, Daiyu passed behind the bed and left through the back courtyard. Xifeng had already entered by the front and asked Baoyu, “Are you feeling any better? If there is anything you feel like eating, send someone to fetch it from my quarters.” Aunt Xue came next. Before long, Grandmother Jia also sent someone to inquire after him. By lamplighting time, Baoyu had taken only two sips of soup before sinking into a heavy, feverish sleep. Then Zhou Rui's wife, Wu Xindeng's wife, Zheng Haoshi's wife, and several other older women who often visited heard that Baoyu had been beaten and came in as well.

p.src: Xiren promised that she would and escorted them out. Just as she was about to return, she saw an old maid sent by Lady Wang, who announced, “Her Ladyship wants one of Second Master's attendants.” On hearing this, Xiren thought for a moment, then turned back and quietly told Qingwen, Sheyue, Tanyun, Qiuwen, and the others, “Her Ladyship has summoned someone. Take good care of things here; I shall be back shortly.” With that, she went straight out of the garden with the old maid and made her way to the main apartments. Lady Wang was seated on a cool couch, fanning herself with a plantain-leaf fan. When Xiren arrived, she said, “It would have done to send anyone at all. Now that you have left him too, who is there to attend him?” Xiren hastened to answer with an obliging smile, “Second Master has only just settled into a sound sleep. Those four or five maids have grown capable now and know how to attend him, so please do not worry, Your Ladyship. I feared that Your Ladyship might have instructions to give, and that if they came they might fail to understand at once and cause a delay.” Lady Wang said, “There are no particular instructions. I only wanted to ask how badly he is hurting now.” Xiren replied, “I applied the medicine Miss Bao sent to Second Master's wounds, and he is somewhat better than before. At first the pain was so severe that he could not lie still, but now he is sleeping soundly, so he must be improving.” Lady Wang asked again, “Has he eaten anything?” Xiren replied, “He took two sips from the bowl of soup the Old Lady sent, but kept complaining of thirst and asking for sour-plum drink. I thought that sour plums have an astringent effect. He had only just been beaten and was not allowed even to cry out, so all that pent-up heat and fevered blood must still be trapped within him. If the drink made it lodge there and brought on a serious illness, what would we do? So after much coaxing I persuaded him not to drink it. Instead, I mixed him some syrup made from candied roses. He took half a bowl, then complained that he was tired of it and that it was not fragrant or sweet enough.” Lady Wang exclaimed, “Oh dear! You should have come and told me sooner. A few days ago someone sent me two bottles of fragrant essence. I had intended to give him some, but I was afraid he would waste it, so I did not. Since he has grown tired of that rose syrup, take these two bottles to him. A single teaspoon stirred into a bowl of water makes it wonderfully fragrant.” Then she called Caiyun and said, “Bring the bottles of fragrant essence that arrived the other day.” Xiren said, “Please bring only two bottles. Any more would merely go to waste. If they prove insufficient, I can always come back and ask for more.” Caiyun went away and, after quite some time, returned with exactly two bottles, which she handed to Xiren. Xiren examined them. They were two small glass bottles, each about three inches tall, with screw-top silver caps. On a pale-yellow label one was inscribed “Pure Osmanthus Essence,” and the other “Pure Rose Essence.”

p.src: Xiren assented and was just about to leave when Lady Wang called her back. “Wait. I have just thought of something I want to ask you.” Xiren hurried back. Seeing that no one else was in the room, Lady Wang asked, “I seem to have heard that Baoyu was beaten today because Huan said something about him to the Master. Have you heard anything about that? If you have, tell me. I will not make a commotion or let anyone know that you told me.” Xiren replied, “I did not hear that. I heard Second Master was beaten because he had kept an actor for himself, and the people who owned him came to demand him back from the Master.” Lady Wang shook her head. “That was one reason, but there was another.” “I truly know nothing of any other reason,” said Xiren. But today I would venture to say something presumptuous before Your Ladyship. Strictly speaking…” Halfway through, she hastily swallowed the rest. “Go on,” said Lady Wang. Xiren smiled. “If Your Ladyship will not be angry, I shall say it.” “Why should I be angry? Say whatever you wish,” replied Lady Wang. Xiren said, “Strictly speaking, Second Master does need the Master to discipline him once or twice. If the Master does not restrain him, there is no telling what he may do in the future.” On hearing this, Lady Wang pressed her palms together and murmured, “Amitabha Buddha!” Then, unable to contain herself, she addressed Xiren tenderly: “My dear child, thank heaven you understand! What you have said is precisely what is in my heart. How could I not know that a son must be disciplined? When your Master Zhu was alive, how strictly I guided him! Do you suppose I no longer know how to raise a son? There is only one reason: I am nearly fifty now, and he is the only son I have left. He has always been frail, and besides, the Old Lady treasures him like a jewel. If I controlled him too strictly and anything happened to him—or if the Old Lady fell ill with anger—the whole household, high and low, would be thrown into turmoil. Would that not make matters worse? And so I have spoiled him through indulgence. Again and again I patiently reason with him, lecture him, then lose my temper and scold him, and finally weep. At the time he behaves better, but afterward it makes no difference. I fear he will not stop until he has suffered for it in earnest. Yet if he is beaten and maimed, whom shall I depend upon in years to come?” As she spoke, tears began to roll down her cheeks.

And those people are only too willing to ingratiate themselves with him, so one can hardly blame him for becoming like this. In the end, it must be that we have failed to advise him properly. Since Your Ladyship has raised the matter today, there is something else that has long weighed on my mind. I have often wanted to report it and ask for your guidance. But I feared Your Ladyship might suspect my motives. Then not only would my words be wasted, but I might be left without even a place to be buried.” Sensing a deeper meaning in her words, Lady Wang asked quickly, “My dear child, whatever it is, speak freely. Lately, hearing everyone praise you both to your face and behind your back, I assumed it was merely because you were attentive to Baoyu and amiable toward everyone—small virtues of that kind. That was why I treated you on the same footing as the old concubines. Who would have thought that everything you have just said is sound and weighty reasoning, exactly in accord with my own thoughts? Say whatever is on your mind. Only be sure that no one else learns of it.” Xiren said, “I have nothing else in particular to say. I only wish to ask Your Ladyship for instructions: could some arrangement be made so that Second Master might move out of the Garden and live outside from now on? That would be best.” Lady Wang was greatly startled. Seizing Xiren’s hand, she asked anxiously, “Has Baoyu been behaving improperly with someone?” Xiren hastily replied, “Please do not be alarmed, Your Ladyship. Nothing of the sort has happened. This is merely my own humble notion. Second Master is grown now, and the young ladies inside are grown as well. Moreover, Miss Lin and Miss Bao are his cousins on the two sides of the family. Though they call one another brother and sisters, there remains the distinction between male and female. It is not proper for them to live and spend their days and nights together, and one cannot help feeling anxious. To outsiders, too, it would not look seemly for a respectable household. As the saying goes, ‘When all is well, think of what might go wrong.’ How many thoughtless people in this world do something quite innocently, only for a calculating observer to take it as deliberate and spread damaging talk about it? It would certainly be unwise not to guard against such things beforehand. Your Ladyship knows Second Master’s usual disposition. He is especially fond of romping among us girls. If no precautions are taken and the slightest impropriety should occur, sooner or later, then whether it was true or false, there would be no silencing so many tongues. What restraint do spiteful people ever show? When pleased, they praise someone as more virtuous than a bodhisattva; when displeased, they revile that same person as worse than a beast.”

p.src: If in the future everyone speaks well of the Second Master, we shall all get by without incident. But if anyone should find a single fault to speak of, then never mind us—even if we were torn limb from limb and burdened with ten thousand crimes, those would be trifles. Yet would not the Second Master's lifelong reputation and character be ruined? And Madam, for her part, would find it difficult to face Master. As the proverb says, ‘A gentleman guards against trouble before it arises.’ It would be best to take precautions now. Madam has so many matters to attend to that naturally this may not have occurred to you at once. It would be excusable if we had not thought of it; but now that we have, our guilt would be all the greater if we failed to report it to Madam. Lately I have worried over this day and night, yet could speak of it to no one; only the lamp knows what has been in my heart.” These words struck Lady Wang like a thunderbolt, touching directly upon the affair of Jinchuan. Her affection and gratitude toward Xiren deepened beyond measure, and she hastily said with a smile, “My dear child, to think you possess such breadth of mind and have considered everything so thoroughly! It is not that the thought never occurred to me; these last few times, other matters made me forget it. What you have said today has reminded me. How good of you to safeguard the reputation and dignity of both mother and son! I truly never knew you were so admirable. Very well, you may go now. I know what must be done. But there is one more thing: since you have spoken so today, I entrust him to you. Watch over him whatever happens. To preserve him is to preserve me. I shall certainly not fail you.” Xiren repeatedly promised that she would and withdrew. When she returned, Baoyu had just awakened, and Xiren reported to him about the fragrant cordial. Baoyu was overjoyed and at once had some mixed for him to taste. It was indeed exceptionally fragrant and delicious. Still preoccupied with Daiyu and eager to send someone to her, he was wary of Xiren. He therefore devised a plan and first sent Xiren to Baochai's quarters to borrow a book.

p.src: Once Xiren had gone, Baoyu summoned Qingwen and instructed her, “Go to Miss Lin's place and see what she is doing. If she asks about me, just say I am better.” Qingwen said, “Why should I go there out of the blue, for no apparent reason? At least give me some message, so that my visit has a proper purpose.” “There is nothing to say,” replied Baoyu. Qingwen said, “Then at least send something or have me fetch something. Otherwise, how am I to account for my going there?” Baoyu thought for a moment, then reached out, picked up two handkerchiefs, and tossed them to Qingwen. Smiling, he said, “Very well. Tell her I sent you to give her these.” “Now that is strange,” said Qingwen. What would she want with two handkerchiefs that are neither new nor properly old? She will only become angry again and say you are making fun of her.” Baoyu smiled. “Do not worry. She will understand.”

p.src: Hearing this, Qingwen had no choice but to take the handkerchiefs to the Naiad's House. She found Chunxian drying handkerchiefs on the railing. Seeing her enter, Chunxian hurriedly waved her hand and said, “She has gone to bed.” Qingwen went inside. The room was pitch-dark. No lamp had been lit. Daiyu was already lying in bed and asked who it was. Qingwen quickly replied, “Qingwen.” “What is it?” asked Daiyu. Qingwen said, “The Second Master has sent these handkerchiefs to you, miss.” At this, Daiyu was bewildered and thought to herself, “Why has he sent me handkerchiefs?” She therefore asked, “Who gave him these handkerchiefs? They must be of the finest quality. Tell him to keep them for someone else; I have no need of such things just now.” Qingwen laughed. “They are not new. They are merely ordinary used ones.” On hearing this, Lin Daiyu became more perplexed than ever. She searched her thoughts with the utmost care and pondered for a while before suddenly understanding. She hastily said, “Put them down and go.” Qingwen had no choice but to set them down and leave. All the way back she puzzled over the matter, unable to understand what it meant.

p.src: Lin Daiyu, meanwhile, had divined the meaning of the handkerchiefs, and her heart and soul began to reel. Baoyu's painstaking thoughtfulness showed that he understood the sorrow in her heart, which filled her with joy; yet she did not know what would become of that sorrow in the future, which filled her with grief. That he should suddenly send her two used handkerchiefs for no apparent reason would have seemed laughable if he had not understood her deepest meaning. Then again, that he should have them secretly conveyed to her by another filled her with fear. And when she reflected that she herself was forever weeping, a futile habit after all, she was filled with shame. As these thoughts chased one another through her mind, all her innermost feelings suddenly seethed and burned. Unable to free herself from the lingering tide of emotion, Daiyu ordered a lamp to be lit. All thought of suspicion or propriety forgotten, she ground ink at the desk, dipped her brush, and swiftly wrote upon the two old handkerchiefs:

p.src: As Lin Daiyu was about to write more, she felt her whole body burning and her face aflame. She went to the dressing mirror, lifted its brocade cover, and looked. Seeing her cheeks crimson, she secretly admired how their beauty surpassed even peach blossoms, never knowing that this was the beginning of an illness. Only after some time did she go to bed, still holding the handkerchiefs and pondering over them. No more need be said of this.

p.src: Now Xiren went to see Baochai, only to find that Baochai was not in the Garden but had gone to visit her mother, so Xiren returned empty-handed. Baochai did not return until the second watch of the night. Baochai had always known Xue Pan's temperament, and already half suspected that he had egged someone on to inform against Baoyu; when she now heard Xiren say the same thing, she became more convinced than ever. In fact, Xiren had heard it from Beiming, and Beiming had merely made a private conjecture without any evidence, yet had decided that Xue Pan must have been the one who told. Xue Pan was blamed only because he had acquired such a reputation over the years. In truth, this time it was not his doing at all, yet everyone firmly accused him, leaving him no way to clear himself. That day he returned after drinking outside, paid his respects to his mother, and found Baochai there. After exchanging a few casual words, he asked, “I hear Cousin Baoyu has come to grief. What happened?” Aunt Xue was already distressed over the matter, and when he asked about it, she said through clenched teeth, “You wretched good-for-nothing! You caused all of this, and you still have the face to ask?” Xue Pan stared at her in astonishment and hurriedly asked, “What have I ever done?” Aunt Xue said, “Still playing the fool! Everyone knows you were the one who told, and you still deny it.” Xue Pan replied, “If everyone said I had murdered someone, would you believe that too?” Aunt Xue said, “Even your sister knows it was you. Surely you don't think she would falsely accuse you too?” Baochai hastened to intervene: “Mother, Brother, please stop shouting. If we all calm down, we can get to the truth of the matter.” Then she turned to Xue Pan and said, “Whether you told or not, the matter is over now. There is no need to argue it out and turn a small affair into a large one. I only advise you to behave less recklessly outside from now on and meddle less in other people's affairs. You spend every day roaming about with that crowd, and you are never on your guard. If nothing happens afterward, well and good. But if anything does happen, even when you had no hand in it, everyone will suspect you. Never mind anyone else—I would be the first to do so.” Xue Pan was by nature blunt and outspoken and could never abide such evasive insinuations. Hearing Baochai urge him to stop going out, while his mother accused him of spreading tales and blamed him for Baoyu's beating, he was already jumping with rage, protesting his innocence with oaths upon his life. He cursed the others as well: “Who is laying such a filthy charge against me? I won't rest until I've knocked that bastard's teeth out! They plainly want to curry favor because Baoyu was beaten, so they are using me as a scapegoat. Is Baoyu some heavenly king? His father gives him one beating, and the whole household has to make a commotion for days.

p.src: That other time, when he had misbehaved and Uncle gave him a couple of blows, the Old Lady somehow heard about it afterward and was told that Cousin Zhen had caused it. She summoned him for no reason and gave him a scolding. And today they have gone so far as to drag me into it! Since they have dragged me in, I'm not afraid. I'll go in there this very minute and beat Baoyu to death. Then I'll pay for his life with mine, and we'll all be rid of the trouble.” Still shouting, he seized a door bar and made to run out. Aunt Xue, thoroughly alarmed, caught hold of him and cried, “You accursed wretch, whom are you going to beat? Beat me first!” Xue Pan's eyes bulged like bronze bells as he shouted, “Why torment me like this? You won't let me go, yet you falsely accuse me for no reason. As long as Baoyu remains alive, I shall bear this slander every day. Better that we all die and have peace.” Baochai also hurried forward to restrain him: “Please control yourself. Mother is beside herself with worry, yet instead of comforting her, you carry on like this. Never mind Mother—even if someone else advised you, it would be for your own good, yet their advice only makes your temper flare up.” Xue Pan said, “Now you talk like that! You were the one who said it all!” Baochai replied, “You only blame me for speaking, but never blame yourself for acting without thought for the consequences.” Xue Pan said, “All you can do is blame me for not considering the consequences. Why don't you blame Baoyu for the way he goes about flirting and stirring up trouble outside? Say no more than this—take that business with Qiguan the other day. We had met Qiguan a dozen times or so, yet I had never exchanged a single intimate word with him. How was it that when Baoyu met him the other day, before he even knew his name, Qiguan gave him his sash? Are you going to say I told about that as well?” Aunt Xue and Baochai cried out anxiously, “Why bring that up again? That was precisely why he was beaten. This proves you were the one who told.” Xue Pan said, “This is enough to make a man die of rage! I am not angry that they blame me for telling. I am angry that a single Baoyu can turn the whole place upside down like this.” Baochai said, “Who has been making a scene? You were the first to seize weapons and start a commotion, yet you accuse everyone else of making one.” Xue Pan found that every word Baochai spoke was reasonable and difficult to refute—harder to answer, indeed, than his mother's words. He therefore sought some remark that would silence her, so that no one would dare oppose him. Being in a fury, he gave no thought to the weight of his words and said, “Dear sister, you needn't quarrel with me. I have long known what is in your heart. Mother once told me that your gold must be matched with someone who has jade to make a proper marriage, and you took it to heart. Now that you see Baoyu has that wretched thing of his, naturally you defend him at every turn.”

p.src: Before he had even finished, Baochai was stunned with anger. Clinging to Aunt Xue, she burst into tears and cried, “Mother, listen to what Brother is saying!” When Xue Pan saw his sister weeping, he knew that he had spoken rashly. Still in a huff, he went to his own room and retired, and nothing more need be said of it.

p.src: Aunt Xue was trembling all over with anger, yet she tried to comfort Baochai, saying, “You know how that wretch usually talks without the least sense. Tomorrow I shall make him apologize to you.” Baochai’s heart was filled with grievance and indignation. She longed to do something about it, but feared distressing her mother; so she had no choice but to take leave of her in tears. They returned separately to their rooms, and Baochai wept the entire night away. When she rose early the next morning, she had no heart for washing or dressing. After putting herself together anyhow, she went out to see her mother. By chance she met Lin Daiyu standing alone beneath the shade of the flowers, and Daiyu asked where she was going. Xue Baochai replied, “Home,” and kept walking as she spoke. Daiyu watched her depart in low spirits and noticed that her eyes bore traces of tears, quite unlike her usual self. u.src: Aunt Xue was trembling all over with anger, yet she tried to comfort Baochai, saying, “You know how that wretch usually talks without the least sense. Tomorrow I shall make him apologize to you.”

Baochai’s heart was filled with grievance and indignation. She longed to do something about it, but feared distressing her mother; so she had no choice but to take leave of her in tears. They returned separately to their rooms, and Baochai wept the entire night away.
When she rose early the next morning, she had no heart for washing or dressing. After putting herself together anyhow, she went out to see her mother.
